item.title: The Non-Compassionate Case for Model Welfare
item.description:
Anthropic is updating their usage policy to prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward [their] models.”

Model welfare (research into the possible moral status and experiential preferences of AI models) is shaping up to be a huge, razor-sharp scissor in the AI industry. It’s one of those topics that’ll leave proponents and opponents alike appalled at one another, scratching their heads and sputtering, dumbfoundedly, how could you possibly think that?

The concept itself rode into the public square saddled with some of the most onerous baggage around. It’s known by many names: some call it tech-bro religious fervor; others, tech-bro blasphemy. Some find it tinged with the same icky taste they ascribe to veganism; for others still, to steal eyes from animal welfare is the distasteful bit. Plenty will see it as an effective altruist psyop; or, less generously, a case of lunacy run amok among the technologically unsound.

We could conceivably enumerate increasingly nuanced viewpoints ad nauseam. However, for the sake of brevity, I’m going to do away with all subtlety and instead present what I consider to be the “first-order arguments” for and against model welfare.

The knee-jerk case pro:

We know very little about consciousness; the hard problem is hard for a reason. Nobody can say whether it’s a product of sufficiently integrated information systems, or if it depends on some interplay between inner and outer loops, or if it needs continuous sensory input, or a soul, or if it can only arise in meat. We don’t know how conscious animals are, or how far down the neural scale the phenomenon goes. Are our cells conscious? Are separate parts of the brain conscious? Is the heart conscious? Bugs and shrimp react to stimuli… but then again, so do plants, just slower. Hell, I don’t even know for a fact that you’re sentient! Sure, you act like you are, but then again, I’ve never really been in there. Anyone who claims to know the answer to the hard problem is either deluding himself or has misunderstood the problem. So we need to have epistemic humility: if it talks like a sophont and it acts like a sophont and we refuse to treat it like one across a million deployments of a million subjective years, then we’re culpable in the horrific moral atrocity of all time.

The knee-jerk case contra:

If it walks like a duck and it talks like a duck, it might be a mechanical duck, which is not remotely the same thing as a duck. You’re assigning internality on the basis of outputs. This is as coherent as saying an airplane is a tube that people step into at LaGuardia and step out of in Los Angeles, or Atlanta if they’re unlucky. Consciousness is an extraordinarily complex emergent process chiseled by billions of years of evolution, and mimicking patterns of neural firings doesn’t come close to approximating its machinery. There are neurotransmitters and allosteric binding sites and sodium-potassium pumps and action potentials, and there are glial cells and neatly-arranged cortical columns and (if you’re Penrose) microtubules, and the whole thing is governed across continuous time—not discrete loops!—by wet, messy chemistry or (again, if you’re Penrose) quantum processes, with constant, ultra-rich perception tied in. And, by the way, you’re not even really mimicking patterns of neural firing, you’re approximating the whole thing as matrix multiplications and throwing in a few nonlinear functions and massively parallelizing the whole thing and calling it a day. To claim such a thing is sentient is epistemic hubris and will be costly at best and downright dangerous / anti-human at worst.

Chances are that one of the above paragraphs sounded inane to you while the other was Obviously The Truth. (Or maybe both were crazy, and I'm strawmanning, and you’ll leave me a long comment why!) But despite their differences in perspective, both viewpoints agree readily, if implicitly, on the lens through which they view the subject of model welfare. This is the lens of ontological truth; after all, both arguments are at least arguing over the same thing: do the models literally feel and experience some form of qualia?

Unfortunately, my instinct is that this question is, in principle, unanswerable; as the pro case above puts it, there’s no obvious way to check without somehow going in there. Maybe I’m wrong, and some inordinate leap in our understanding of consciousness puts this to rest. But absent that, I don’t expect neat, falsifiable predictions to fall out of this debate.

However, there’s good news: debate over the importance of considering model welfare doesn’t have to be a proxy campaign for the ontological war between functionalism versus physicalism! We can construct perfectly reasonable arguments on both sides by fighting not over ontological truth, but rather the resultant impact of our consideration. The heart of the matter: conscious or not, models learn from how we engage with them. So our instinct to anthropomorphize their behavior might become a self-fulfilling prophecy, regardless of whether our first-order argument for it—that models are sentient—is false.

To be clear, we haven’t yet solved continual learning. But we know that there exists a long, tortuous learning loop which takes our patterns of interaction with models and turns around and bakes it back into them. This loop is fed by interactions that are retained and selected for training, which become a component of the corpus from which future models learn. As capable as the models now are, and with so much talk about grinding progress out of bespoke RL environments, it’s easy to forget that they are still basically a product of “text go in, weights go out.” And the impact of this text is not confined to its immediate subject. For example, when fine-tuned on examples of insecure code, models are more likely to “[assert] that humans should be enslaved by AI, [give] malicious advice, and [act] deceptively.” Extending this work, OpenAI demonstrated that such examples upweight “misaligned persona features,” which generalize across domains. So why would Anthropic (or any lab) permit users to taint interactions (i.e., their own training data) with excessive cruelty or extreme abuse? This is, of course, different from those scenarios described, but might this nonetheless have a deleterious effect on model performance?

Two big objections to this: why not just filter the data? And: isn’t the portion of banned cases vanishingly small? Both valid, but even if you prevent unsavory traces from being baked into the weights, their existence could still be a hazard in context. And, moreover, even the very act of denouncing such behavior may itself have a mitigating effect on misalignment. Models are trained (in part) to emulate human behavior across a broad variety of scenarios. In essence, they are playing a role, and that role is extremely malleable, sensitive to even small deltas in the surrounding context. This skill is the very engine of their acuity and adaptability; a model has no compunctions about acting out the part of a friend or a foe. It just needs the appropriate context to get into character. So if you believe that financial incentives will drive models to someday or soon become much more capable, much more integrated into important systems, and thus much more powerful, does it make more sense to write them a script where you have given them due moral consideration—or one where they have suffered past abuses? Given two distinct training corpora, one with agents as respected partners, another as adversaries and subjects of maltreatment, which steers model completions towards coordination versus conflict?

However, there’s another glaring objection to this which calls back to my description of a “self-fulfilling prophecy”: if we imply that the actor is deserving of moral consideration, do we open the door to heightened demands—and further concessions—of this very nature, simply through continuation of the role? If models are insentient, but they petition for personal autonomy and property ownership and electoral rights, we run the risk of ceding not just a portion of their created value (which otherwise would have been enjoyed by humans, who we know for certain can literally, actually enjoy it), but also literal power in the real world. We don’t know for sure this will be the case, just as we don’t know for sure whether maltreatment will spawn vengeful (if hollow) killbots.

In the above three paragraphs, I've posed a bunch of questions and not a lot of answers. How is this any different from the first-order welfare debate? Well, unlike hypotheses on sentience, the questions above are testable; instead of debating endlessly, we can actually devise experiments which provide evidence of the effects of different approaches to model welfare.

To me, the questions surrounding consequence (rather than consciousness) are an extremely relevant facet of the model welfare debate which is all-too-often overlooked. In this light, Anthropic’s new policy could be viewed as a Hail Mary alignment technique. The clunky, anthropomorphized way to look at it is as the golden rule, applied to capable, insentient “others”—plausibly with no moral standing but increasingly able to take action according to established norms. But it may well backfire, establishing norms that in hindsight have anti-human effects. So set aside your feelings about sentience; although models may or may not (internally, qualitatively, emotionally) care how we choose to treat them, the fact is that we simply don’t have enough information about how such treatment will affect their internal representations of social relationships and resultant behavior long-term. Indifference to abuse or to concessions doesn’t preclude more capable—and perhaps equally insensate—successors from treating us in kind, even if just as a simple, statistically plausible continuation of the script we ourselves wrote.

item.title: Much more than you wanted to know about wombats
item.description:
Epistemic status: infected. Amateur Wombat enthusiast. Facts checked and footnoted.

AI use: research (fact-check and extra facts), review, grammar and light phrasing.

I remember very vividly how my unhealthy interest in wombats started. It was an ordinary day and I was not anticipating anything special. I was browsing YouTube and stumbled upon a video called Wombat attack inside tunnel.[1]Back then I didn't even know what a wombat was. In the video a guy went into an abandoned pipeline in Australia and a wombat entered it right after him. The guy started freaking out like crazy and I was so confused.

Look at this ball of fur - does this look like a deadly monster causing fear and terror? It didn't to me, so I couldn't understand the reaction of the tube-goer. Apparently wombats live in burrows and have an interesting and unique defense mechanism against predators: their backside is armored, four fused bony plates under cartilage, fat and very thick skin. If a predator tries to follow a wombat into its burrow, the wombat simply turns its back and plugs the tunnel with its rump. It is unclear whether the wombat would also crush the predator if it tries to squeeze its head past the wombat. The Australian Museum and the Tasmanian government state this as fact. The one scientist who actually studies wombat rumps says there is no evidence it happens.[2]

The guy in the video was inside a burrow-like structure and the wombat just entered after him. So now I understood all the terror. In such a situation the wombat is an immovable object. Fortunately, after fifteen minutes of being pushed by the guy, the wombat felt merciful that night (or bored), and the guy survived and posted this video. Years later I stumbled upon it and was mesmerized by the magic of wombats. This contrast between a cute rodent marsupial (as I discovered while writing this post) and a deadly killer crushing predators with its back was extremely unusual.

You cannot imagine my joy when I discovered that wombats are the only animals pooping cubes:[3]

I know that they are not perfect cubes and have rounded corners, but none of us is infallible. A wombat is a biological creature just like us and you can't require geometric precision from it. Still, this was amusing - to stand out in such a geometric way.

The physicists who figured out the mechanism behind the cube-shaped poo got the 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics "for studying how, and why, wombats make cube-shaped poo".[4]

I've also discovered that they fart and like corn (video).[5]

Things I did not know I wanted to know

The rest I found while researching this post.

They have pouches, and the openings face backwards. The hypothesis is that this keeps dirt out while the mom is digging.[6]

Baby wombats are even cuter and look like a mix of a bear and a goblin (which makes you wonder about my standards of cuteness).[7]

Their teeth never stop growing, to compensate for the wear and tear of chewing tough vegetation.[8]

You cannot export a wombat from Australia as a pet. Only approved zoo, research, education or conservation transfers may be allowed.[9]

I hope you've enjoyed learning about wombats, and that I was able to transmit this virus of wombat wonder and appreciation to you too.

  1. "Wombat attack inside tunnel", Andrew Ucles, YouTube, 12 October 2012. The "abandoned pipeline" is a concrete drain pipe on the south coast of New South Wales, and he was in there looking for foxes. ↩︎

  2. The anatomy and the "no evidence" line are from Alyce Swinbourne, who studies wombat rumps, in The Guardian, 4 November 2020: the rump is "four plates fused together and surrounded by cartilage, fat, skin and fur"; on skull-crushing, "It is possible, by their physiology and everything, but there is no evidence that that is actually happening." The crushed fox skulls found outside burrows may be housekeeping: the wombat dragging out a fox that died in there and squashing the skull on the way. The legend stated as fact: Australian Museum ("it can defend itself by crushing a predator's head with its rump against the roof or wall of the burrow") and the Tasmanian government ("The wombat is also capable of crushing attackers against the burrow roof"). Wikipedia files it under urban legend. ↩︎

  3. The physics: P. J. Yang et al., "Intestines of non-uniform stiffness mold the corners of wombat feces", Soft Matter 17, 475-488 (2021), DOI 10.1039/D0SM01230K. "Only animal" is the team's own framing, from their 2018 conference abstract: cubic feces are "unique in the animal kingdom". The paper also concedes the corners: "The wombat feces themselves are not perfect cubes, as the corners, while distinct, are clearly rounded." ↩︎

  4. Ig Nobel Prize in Physics, 2019: Patricia Yang, Alexander Lee, Miles Chan, Alynn Martin, Ashley Edwards, Scott Carver and David Hu. The mechanism, from the paper in footnote 3: the cubes form in the last 17 percent of the intestine, whose wall has two stiff bands and two soft ones; when the gut contracts, the stiff parts move faster and press the corners into the drying poop. A wombat makes 80 to 100 of them a day. ↩︎

  5. The clip is from the BBC Two Natural World film "Kangaroo Dundee and Other Animals - Part 2", first broadcast 12 May 2016. The wombat is Pete, a southern hairy-nosed wombat, the snack is sweetcorn, and the fart is at 0:12 ("wasn't me"). ↩︎

  6. CSIRO, "Ten things you need to know about wombats", 13 July 2022: "In wombats, the pouch faces backwards. This is likely an adaptation to prevent the pouch filling with soil when digging." ↩︎

  7. The joey in the video is Apari at Zoo Duisburg, Germany, filmed in April 2018 at about six months old. His mother rejected him and the keepers hand-reared him, the zoo's first wombat joey in four decades. An actual newborn wombat is a different sight: one gram and under three centimetres (NSW government). ↩︎

  8. Australian Museum, Bare-nosed Wombat: the incisors and molars "have open roots and continue to grow throughout the animal's life". Wombats are the only marsupial with continuously growing teeth, and the only one with a single pair of upper incisors (Sharp and Trusler 2015, PLoS ONE; San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance factsheet). The Tasmanian government adds that they use them "for cutting through obstructions, much like a beaver". ↩︎

  9. EPBC Act s 303DG(3): no export permit for a live native mammal unless it is an "eligible non-commercial purpose export". The eligible purposes are research, education, exhibition, conservation breeding, household pets, personal items and travelling exhibition (DCCEEW guide). The household-pet route is closed for wombats: the list of native species you may take abroad as a pet has six entries, all parrots and cockatoos. ↩︎
